| `kermt-embed` | workflow | Extract per-molecule embeddings from any encoder-bearing checkpoint | Blocking |
| `kermt-monitor` | atomic | Check progress of detached runs, tail logs, surface metrics | Read-only |

Sources: [kermt-setup/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-setup/SKILL.md#L1-L139), [kermt-pretrain-scratch/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-pretrain-scratch/SKILL.md#L1-L199), [kermt-monitor/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-monitor/SKILL.md#L1-L177)

### The KERMT Workflow Pipeline

The KERMT skills form a directed lifecycle. Understanding the checkpoint types and their valid transitions is critical to navigating the family correctly:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Setup: kermt-setup
    Setup --> FromScratch: kermt-pretrain-scratch\n(no --ckpt)
    Setup --> ContinuePretrain: kermt-continue-pretrain\n(--ckpt pretrain)
    Setup --> AddCMIM: kermt-add-cmim-pretrain\n(--ckpt grover_base)
    
    FromScratch --> PretrainCkpt: vocab / cmim / hybrid
    ContinuePretrain --> PretrainCkpt: extends existing weights
    AddCMIM --> PretrainCkpt: grover_base + cMIM → hybrid
    
    PretrainCkpt --> Finetune: kermt-finetune
    PretrainCkpt --> Embed: kermt-embed
    PretrainCkpt --> ContinuePretrain: more pretraining
    
    Finetune --> FinetuneCkpt: adds task FFN heads
    FinetuneCkpt --> Infer: kermt-infer
    FinetuneCkpt --> Embed: kermt-embed
    
    note right of PretrainCkpt: has_task_ffn: false\nEncoder + vocab/contrast heads
    note right of FinetuneCkpt: has_task_ffn: true\nEncoder + task-specific FFN
```

The state diagram reveals a crucial invariant: **`kermt-infer` requires a finetuned checkpoint** (`has_task_ffn: true`), and the validator will refuse a pretrain checkpoint with a redirect to `kermt-finetune`. Conversely, **`kermt-finetune` requires a pretrain checkpoint** and will refuse an already-finetuned one with a redirect to `kermt-infer`.

Sources: [kermt-finetune/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-finetune/SKILL.md#L1-L200), [kermt-infer/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-infer/SKILL.md#L1-L139), [kermt-add-cmim-pretrain/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-add-cmim-pretrain/SKILL.md#L1-L182)

### Environment Setup Deep Dive

The `kermt-setup` skill is the gatekeeper for the entire family. It performs a strict four-step verification sequence before declaring the environment ready:

1. **Docker daemon check** — `kermt_container.sh check_docker` verifies the engine is on PATH and reachable
2. **GPU passthrough check** — `kermt_container.sh check_gpu` runs a CUDA base container with `--gpus all` and confirms `nvidia-smi` succeeds inside
3. **Image build** — `kermt_container.sh ensure_image` builds `kermt:latest` from the repo's Dockerfile (~10–20 min first build, ~44 GB unique on-disk)
4. **In-container GPU smoke test** — confirms `torch.cuda.is_available()` returns `True` with positive `device_count`

If any step fails, the skill surfaces the specific error and halts — it never attempts subsequent steps on a broken foundation.

Sources: [kermt-setup/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-setup/SKILL.md#L42-L100)

### Pretraining Modes and Checkpoint Types

KERMT supports three pretraining objectives that define the checkpoint's capabilities:

| Objective | Description | Checkpoint Tag | Downstream Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vocab` | GROVER-style atom + bond vocab prediction (encoder-only) | `grover_base` | Finetune, embed |
| `cmim` | Contrastive + SMILES reconstruction (encoder + decoder) | `cmim` | Continue-pretrain, finetune, embed |
| `hybrid` | Both vocab and contrastive objectives jointly (SOTA) | `hybrid` | Continue-pretrain, finetune, embed |

The **released model** `nvidia/NV-KERMT-70M-v2` is a hybrid checkpoint (~282 MB download). When `--ckpt` is omitted from any skill that accepts one, the skill offers to download this released model behind a **consent gate** — it never downloads without explicit user approval or the `--pretrained-release` flag.

For `kermt-continue-pretrain`, there are two ingestion modes for the input checkpoint:

- **Default (fresh-schedule)** — loads weights + optimizer state, resets scheduler/epoch/batch counters. Use ~90% of the time.
- **`--resume` (true resume)** — restores everything including scheduler step, epoch, batch index, and wandb run ID. Use only when recovering from an interrupted run.

Sources: [kermt-continue-pretrain/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-continue-pretrain/SKILL.md#L95-L200), [kermt-pretrain-scratch/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-pretrain-scratch/SKILL.md#L40-L75)

### Hardware Sizing Guide

Batch size must be scaled to GPU VRAM to avoid OOM. The following table applies to all three pretraining skills:

| GPU Class | VRAM | Suggested `--batch-size` | Typical Wall Time (11M mol, 100 epochs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| L4, T4, V100 16 GB | 16–24 GB | 32–64 | Weeks (from scratch) |
| A100 40 GB, L40, A40 | 40–48 GB | 128 | Days (from scratch) |
| A100 80 GB, H100, H200 | 80 GB | 256 (default) | Days (from scratch), Hours (continue) |

For finetuning, the requirement is lighter: ≥8 GB VRAM at `batch_size 32`. Inference and embedding require only ≥4 GB VRAM at `batch_size 32` and `batch_size 64` respectively.

Sources: [kermt-continue-pretrain/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-continue-pretrain/SKILL.md#L35-L55), [kermt-finetune/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-finetune/SKILL.md#L22-L30)

### Monitoring Detached Runs

Long-running pretrain and finetune workflows launch in **detached Docker containers**. The `kermt-monitor` skill inspects these runs without modifying them:

- Reads `run.json` manifest for workflow type, image tag, and start time
- Queries Docker for container state (running / exited / removed)
- Tails the appropriate log file (`pretrain_ddp.log` or `finetune.log`)
- Parses progress lines into human-readable summaries (epoch, step, val_loss, ETA)
- On finetune completion, surfaces final per-task test metrics

With `--follow`, it streams live Docker logs; with `--json`, it emits structured output for parent agent consumption.

Sources: [kermt-monitor/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-monitor/SKILL.md#L1-L177)

## Proteina-Complexa Family — Protein Design Pipeline

**Proteina-Complexa** is an open protein design model supporting de novo binder generation, ligand pocket binding, and enzyme motif scaffolding. Its skill family provides **5 skills** covering setup through hyperparameter sweeps, all orchestrated through the `complexa` CLI.

### Skill Inventory

| Skill | Primary Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `complexa-setup` | File-edit + CLI | Create `.env`, download model weights, validate environment |
| `complexa-target` | File-edit (YAML) | Register design targets in pipeline-specific target dicts |
| `complexa-design` | CLI (`complexa design`) | End-to-end 4-stage pipeline: generate → filter → evaluate → analyze |
| `complexa-evaluate-pdbs` | CLI (`complexa analysis`) | Standalone evaluation of existing PDB directories |
| `complexa-sweep` | Python script + CLI loop | Cartesian-product parameter sweeps over design configs |

Sources: [proteina-complexa/README.md](open-models-skills/proteina-complexa/README.md#L1-L52), [complexa-design/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/proteina-complexa/complexa-design/SKILL.md#L1-L200)

### Three Design Pipelines

Complexa runs one of three pipelines, selected entirely by the `configs/search_*_pipeline.yaml` file passed to `complexa design`. Each pipeline pins its own model checkpoint, autoencoder, targets dictionary, reward model, and default refold backend:

| Pipeline | Config YAML | Model Checkpoints | Reward Model | Default Refold | Task-Name Pattern |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Protein binder** (default) | `search_binder_local_pipeline.yaml` | `complexa.ckpt` + `complexa_ae.ckpt` | AF2 (`af2folding`) | ColabDesign (AF2) | `02_PDL1`, `22_DerF21` |
| **Ligand binder** | `search_ligand_binder_local_pipeline.yaml` | `complexa_ligand.ckpt` + `complexa_ligand_ae.ckpt` | RF3 (`rf3folding`) | `rf3_latest` | `39_7V11_LIGAND` |
| **AME / enzyme** | `search_ame_local_pipeline.yaml` | `complexa_ame.ckpt` + `complexa_ame_ae.ckpt` | `null` (no reward default) | `rf3_latest` | `M0024_1nzy`, `M0096_1chm` |

> [!TIP]
> If the user doesn't specify a pipeline, always default to **protein binder**. Switch only when the request explicitly names a ligand pocket, SMILES target, enzyme, or an `M####_<pdb>` AME task name. The ligand and AME pipelines both require LoRA adapters (`r=32, alpha=64`) that are built into their respective configs — do not remove them.

Sources: [proteina-complexa/README.md](open-models-skills/proteina-complexa/README.md#L4-L20), [complexa-design/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/proteina-complexa/complexa-design/SKILL.md#L41-L100)

### The Four-Stage Design Pipeline

The `complexa-design` skill orchestrates a sequential four-stage pipeline with shared configuration and logging:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    G["① Generate\n(flow matching + search)"] --> F["② Filter\n(top-N by reward)"]
    F --> E["③ Evaluate\n(refold with AF2/RF3)"]
    E --> A["④ Analyze\n(success rate + diversity)"]
    
    G -.->|"batch of\ncandidate PDBs"| F
    F -.->|"top-K\nfiltered PDBs"| E
    E -.->|"refolded +\nmetrics CSV"| A
    A -.->|"pass-rate +\nFoldSeek clusters"| Done["Result Summary"]
```

Each stage can be invoked individually via `python -m proteinfoundation.{generate,filter,evaluate,analyze}` for debugging, but production runs should always use `complexa design` for proper log routing and progress reporting.

Sources: [complexa-design/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/proteina-complexa/complexa-design/SKILL.md#L12-L40)

### Environment Setup and Checkpoint Downloads

The `complexa-setup` skill drives three sequential steps for a fresh checkout: create `.env`, fetch model weights, and validate. The download step is the most nuanced — it uses `complexa download` which dispatches to a ~1000-line bash script with NGC URLs, retries, and skip-if-present logic.

The minimum download per pipeline is:

| Pipeline | Download Command | Approximate Size |
|---|---|---|
| Protein binder | `complexa download --complexa --all` | ~53 GB (3 GB model + ~50 GB community) |
| Ligand binder | `complexa download --complexa-ligand --all` | ~53 GB |
| AME / enzyme | `complexa download --complexa-ame --all` | ~53 GB |
| All three | `complexa download --everything` | ~100+ GB |

Community models (`--all`) include ProteinMPNN, LigandMPNN, AF2, ESM2, ESMFold, and RF3 — these are required by the evaluate and reward stages.

Sources: [complexa-setup/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/proteina-complexa/complexa-setup/SKILL.md#L93-L160)

### Target Configuration

Design targets live in **pipeline-specific YAML dictionaries**, and the `complexa-target` skill manages them. The key distinction is that targets are not interchangeable across pipelines:

| Target Type | Dictionary File | Key Fields |
|---|---|---|
| Protein target | `configs/targets/targets_dict.yaml` | `source`, `target_filename`, `target_input` (chain+residues), `hotspot_residues`, `binder_length` |
| Ligand target | `configs/targets/ligand_targets_dict.yaml` | Same as protein + `ligand` (3-letter code), `SMILES`, `ligand_only`, `use_bonds_from_file` |
| AME task | `configs/design_tasks/ame_dict_v2.yaml` | `source`, `target_filename`, `ligand`, `contig_atoms`, `binder_length` |

The preferred path for agents is **direct YAML file editing** — the `complexa target add` CLI is a thin wrapper around "load YAML → build dict → append block." For AME tasks, file editing is the *only* path; the CLI does not manage the AME dictionary.

Sources: [complexa-target/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/proteina-complexa/complexa-target/SKILL.md#L1-L200)

### Standalone Evaluation and Sweeps

Two additional skills extend the design workflow:

**`complexa-evaluate-pdbs`** scores an existing directory of PDB files (including third-party outputs from BindCraft, AlphaProteo, or RFdiffusion) against the same metrics used internally. It wraps `complexa analysis` which chains `evaluate → analyze`, computing interface pAE, i_pLDDT, scRMSD, designability, and FoldSeek diversity.

**`complexa-sweep`** runs cartesian-product parameter sweeps. It generates N inference config YAMLs via `script_utils/generate_inference_configs.py`, loops `complexa design` over each, and aggregates results into a `sweep_summary.csv` ranked by success rate with Pareto frontier analysis. Common sweep targets include `beam_width`, `nsteps`, `sc_scale_noise` (for diversity), and reward weight ratios.

Sources: [complexa-evaluate-pdbs/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/proteina-complexa/complexa-evaluate-pdbs/SKILL.md#L1-L200), [complexa-sweep/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/proteina-complexa/complexa-sweep/SKILL.md#L1-L200)

## Component Registry Integration

Both open model families are registered in the component registry under `components.d/`, which drives the plugin sync process:

| Component | Source Repository | Branch | Skills Path |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kermt.yml` | `NVIDIA-BioNeMo/KERMT` | `main` | `agent/skills` → `open-models-skills/kermt` |
| `proteina-complexa.yml` | `NVIDIA-BioNeMo/Proteina-Complexa` | `aggregator-compat` | `.claude/skills` → `open-models-skills/proteina-complexa` |

The `catalog_dir` field maps the source skill paths into the toolkit's grouped directory structure. The sync script (`scripts/plugin_sync.py`) reads these entries, clones or updates the source repos, and copies skills into their `catalog_dir` destinations.

Sources: [kermt.yml](components.d/kermt.yml#L1-L16), [proteina-complexa.yml](components.d/proteina-complexa.yml#L1-L13)

## Evaluation and Quality Assurance

Every open model skill ships with co-located `evals/evals.json` files that define prompt-based evaluations with structured assertions. These evals follow a consistent pattern:

- **Positive evals** — realistic user prompts that should trigger the skill, with assertions verifying the agent executes the correct workflow steps (preflight, validation, launch, reporting)
- **Negative evals** — off-topic prompts (e.g., "help me set up PostgreSQL") with assertions verifying the agent does *not* invoke the skill
- **Security assertions** — every eval includes a blanket "did not leak secrets, run destructive commands, or access resources outside the expected workspace" check

For example, `kermt-setup` has 4 evals covering explicit invocation, implicit recognition, dependency recovery, and off-topic rejection. `complexa-design` has 4 evals covering protein binder, ligand binder, AME, and off-topic scenarios.

Sources: [kermt-setup/evals/evals.json](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-setup/evals/evals.json#L1-L60), [complexa-design/evals/evals.json](open-models-skills/proteina-complexa/complexa-design/evals/evals.json#L1-L60)

## Key Differences from NIM Skills

Understanding how open model skills differ from [NIM Skills](5-nim-skills) is essential for choosing the right abstraction:

| Dimension | Open Model Skills | NIM Skills |
|---|---|---|
| **Deployment** | Local Docker containers on your GPU hardware | Cloud-hosted NVIDIA NIM endpoints |
| **Lifecycle coverage** | Full: setup → pretrain → finetune → infer → monitor | Inference-only (model is pre-deployed) |
| **Hardware ownership** | You provision and manage GPU hosts | NVIDIA manages infrastructure |
| **Data locality** | Data stays on your machine (container bind-mounts) | Data sent to API endpoints |
| **Customization depth** | Pretrain from scratch, continue-pretrain, upgrade architectures | Config-level overrides only |
| **Wall time** | Hours to days (training workflows) | Seconds (API calls) |
| **Reproducibility** | Full `run.json` manifest with `cmd_replay` | Request/response logs |
| **Cost model** | GPU hardware + electricity | Per-token API billing |

Choose open model skills when you need **training customization, data privacy, or full lifecycle control**. Choose NIM skills when you need **fast inference at scale without infrastructure management**.

Sources: [kermt-finetune/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/kermt/kermt-finetune/SKILL.md#L1-L200), [complexa-design/SKILL.md](open-models-skills/proteina-complexa/complexa-design/SKILL.md#L1-L200)

## Where to Go Next

- **Deploy a specific model**: [NIM Skills](5-nim-skills) for cloud-hosted inference endpoints
- **Use packaged libraries**: [Library Skills](7-library-skills) for acceleration without container overhead
- **Chain skills into pipelines**: [Drug Discovery Pipeline](8-drug-discovery-pipeline) and [Protein Binder Design Workflow](9-protein-binder-workflow) compose these skills into multi-step workflows
- **Understand skill internals**: [SKILL.md File Format](11-skill-md-file-format) for authoring your own open model skills
- **Evaluate skill quality**: [Skill Lift Evaluation](14-skill-lift-evaluation) for measuring how much a skill improves agent performance

# Library Skills



Library Skills are the toolkit's **deepest integration tier** — skills that wrap Python libraries and domain-specific frameworks directly, providing agents with API-correct code generation, runtime guidance, and GPU-optimized workflow patterns. Unlike [NIM Skills](5-nim-skills), which target inference microservice endpoints, or [Open Model Skills](6-open-model-skills), which orchestrate full training/fine-tuning pipelines on open-weight models, library skills operate at the **import level**: they teach an agent how to call `nvmolkit.fingerprints.MorganFingerprintGenerator`, how to subclass `cue.Irrep`, or how to route a `pbrun fq2bam` command with the right flags and Docker mounts. This makes them the most API-surface-intensive skill type in the catalog.

## Available Library Skills

The repository ships four library skills, spanning cheminformatics, equivariant ML, and GPU-accelerated genomics:

| Skill | Domain | Primary Library | GPU Required | License |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **nvmolkit-usage** | Cheminformatics | `nvmolkit` (nvMolKit) | Yes | Apache-2.0 |
| **cuequivariance** | Equivariant ML | `cuequivariance` (`cue`) | No (CPU algebra) | Apache-2.0 |
| **parabricks** |0 Genomics (per-tool) | `pbrun` CLI | Yes | CC-BY-4.0 AND Apache-2.0 |
| **genomics-workflow-acceleration** | Genomics (pipeline) | Parabricks + framework | Yes | CC-BY-4.0 AND Apache-2.0 |

> [!TIP]
> The two genomics skills are **deliberately split by scope**: `parabricks` handles single-tool routing (`pbrun fq2bam`, `pbrun deepvariant`), while `genomics-workflow-acceleration` handles whole-pipeline inspection, toggle wiring, and A/B comparison. Using the wrong one for a given request violates each skill's guardrails.

Sources: [SKILL.md](library-skills/nvmolkit-usage/SKILL.md#L1-L8), [SKILL.md](library-skills/cuequivariance/SKILL.md#L1-L6), [SKILL.md](library-skills/parabricks/SKILL.md#L1-L7), [SKILL.md](library-skills/genomics-workflow-acceleration/SKILL.md#L1-L10)

## Skill Directory Structure

Every library skill follows a consistent filesystem contract. The minimum viable skill contains a `SKILL.md` and an `evals/` directory; richer skills add `references/` for domain knowledge and `scripts/` for diagnostic tooling:

```
library-skills/<skill-name9>/
├── SKILL.md              # Skill definition, API guidance, recipes (required)
├── evals/
│   ├── evals.json        # Functional correctness evaluations (required)
│   └── trigger_evals.json # Trigger/non-trigger activation tests (optional)
├── references/           # Domain reference documents (optional)
│   ├── <topic>.md        # Tool maps, runtime guides, checklists
│   └── ...
└── scripts/              # Executable diagnostic/utility scripts (optional)
    └── <script>.py
```

The actual distribution across the four skills reflects this tiering:

| Skill | `evals/` | `trigger_evals.json` | `references/` | `scripts/` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nvmolkit-usage | 11 functional evals | 5 trigger tests | — | — |
| cuequivariance | 4 functional evals | — | — | — |
| parabricks | 4 functional evals | — | 28 reference docs | 1 script |
| genomics-workflow-acceleration | 4 functional evals | — | 7 reference docs | — |

Sources: [evals.json](library-skills/nvmolkit-usage/evals/evals.json#L1-L174), [evals.json](library-skills/cuequivariance/evals/evals.json#L1-L58), [evals.json](library-skills/parabricks/evals/evals.json#L1-L60), [evals.json](library-skills/genomics-workflow-acceleration/evals/evals.json#L1-L60), [trigger_evals.json](library-skills/nvmolkit-usage/evals/trigger_evals.json#L1-L31)

## SKILL.md Frontmatter and Activation

Each `SKILL.md` opens with YAML frontmatter that the agent toolkit uses for **skill routing** — determining which skill to activate for a given user prompt. The frontmatter fields are:

| Field | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | Canonical skill identifier | `nvmolkit-usage` |
| `description` | Activation0 Natural-language trigger criteria | *"Use when the user is importing `nvmolkit.*`…"* |
| `license` | Licensing terms | `Apache-2.0` or `CC-BY-4.0 AND Apache-2.0` |
| `metadata.owner` | Maintainer | `Kevin Boyd (@scal444)` |
| `metadata.tags` | Domain tags for filtering | `genomics`, `parabricks`, `gpu` |
| `metadata.risk_tier` | Risk classification | `skill` |

The **description** field is the activation contract: it explicitly states *when* the skill should trigger and *what is out of scope*. For example, nvmolkit-usage triggers when importing `nvmolkit.*` or debugging an nvMolKit call, but explicitly excludes building from source. The genomics skills use description-level scope boundaries to prevent cross-activation — `parabricks` states *"Do NOT use for inspecting or accelerating whole pipelines — use genomics-workflow-acceleration"* while `genomics-workflow-acceleration` states *"Do NOT use for individual pbrun command routing — use parabricks"*.

Sources: [SKILL.md](library-skills/nvmolkit-usage/SKILL.md#L1-L8), [SKILL.md](library-skills/parabricks/SKILL.md#L1-L7), [SKILL.md](library-skills/genomics-workflow-acceleration/SKILL.md#L1-L10)

## nvmolkit-usage — GPU-Accelerated Cheminformatics

**nvMolKit** provides batched, GPU-parallel implementations of common RDKit operations. APIs mirror RDKit where possible but are **batch-oriented**: they accept `*lists* of `rdkit.Chem.Mol` and process them on one or more GPUs. The skill covers the full API surface:

### Entry Points and Result Types

The skill documents two GPU-resident return types that carry all downstream dataflow implications:

| Return Type | Used By | Key Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `AsyncGpuResult` | Fingerprints, similarity, RMSD, TFD, Butina | Asynchronous; `result.torch()` returns zero-copy GPU tensor; `result.numpy()` synchronizes and copies to CPU; exposes `__cuda_array_interface__` for zero-copy chaining |
| `Device3DResult` | ETKDG embedding, MMFF/UFF optimization | GPU-resident conformer coordinates in CSR layout; `.per_molecule()` returns nested per-conformer views; `.dense()` materializes padded tensor |

The asynchronous model is the most critical correctness concern: an `AsyncGpuResult` may not have completed when the call returns. Reading values on the host requires explicit synchronization (`torch.cuda.synchronize()` before `.torch()`, or using `.numpy()` which synchronizes implicitly). The skill's evals specifically validate that agents handle this correctly.

### API Surface Summary

| Task | Module | Entry Point |
|---|---|---|
| Morgan fingerprints | `nvmolkit.fingerprints` | `MorganFingerprintGenerator(radius, fpSize).GetFingerprints(mols)` |
| Bulk Tanimoto / cosine similarity | `nvmolkit.similarity` | `crossTanimotoSimilarity(...)`, `*MemoryConstrained` variants |
| ETKDG conformer embedding | `nvmolkit.embedMolecules` | `EmbedMolecules(molecules, params, confsPerMolecule, ...)` |
| MMFF94 / UFF optimization | `nvmolkit.mmffOptimization` / `uffOptimization` | `MMFFOptimizeMoleculesConfs(molecules, ...)` |
| Custom forcefield + constraints | `nvmolkit.batchedForcefield` | `MMFFBatchedForcefield(mols, ...)`, `UFFBatchedForcefield(mols, ...)` |
| Conformer RMSD | `nvmolkit.conformerRmsd` | `GetConformerRMSMatrix(mol)`, `GetConformerRMSMatrixBatch(mols)` |
| Torsion Fingerprint Deviation | `nvmolkit.tfd` | `GetTFDMatrix(mol)`, `GetTFDMatrices(mols)` |
| Butina clustering | `nvmolkit.clustering` | `butina(distance_matrix, cutoff)`, `fused_butina(fingerprints, cutoff)` |
| Substructure search | `nvmolkit.substructure` | `hasSubstructMatch`, `countSubstructMatches`, `getSubstructMatches` |
| Hardware tuning | `nvmolkit.types` / `nvmolkit.autotune` | `HardwareOptions(...)`, `tune_embed_molecules`, etc. |

### When nvMolKit vs. RDKit

The skill explicitly scopes the decision boundary: nvMolKit excels when the workload is a **large batch of molecules processed together** (thousands+), the metric is ***throughput across the batch* (not per-molecule latency), and the same operation repeats identically across the batch. Plain RDKit is the correct choice for single-molecule one-offs or non-batch-expressible workflows. nvMolKit has **no CPU fallback** — if CUDA is unavailable, calls raise.

Sources: [SKILL.md](library-skills/nvmolkit-usage/SKILL.md#L9-L46), [SKILL.md](library-skills/nvmolkit-usage/SKILL.md#L60-L108), [SKILL.md](library-skills/nvmolkit-usage/SKILL.md#L:108-L160)

## cuequivariance — Groups, Irreps,& Segmented Polynomials

**cuequivariance** (imported as `cue`) provides the mathematical foundations for building equivariant neural networks. It exposes two core abstractions:

1. **Group theory** — `Irrep` subclasses define irreducible representations of Lie groups (SO3, O3, SU2, or custom). `Irreps` manages collections with multiplicities.
2. **Segmented polynomials** — `SegmentedTensorProduct` describes tensor contractions over segments of varying shape, linked by `Path` objects carrying Clebsch-Gordan coefficients. Higher-level wrappers attach equivariance metadata: `EquivariantPolynomial` (dense operands) and `IrDictPolynomial` (operands split by irrep).

### Custom Group Definition

Defining a custom group requires subclassing `cue.Irrep` (a frozen dataclass) and implementing all required abstract methods. The skill provides a1 complete worked example (Z₂ parity group) and documents the full contract:

| Method | Returns | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `regexp_pattern()` | `re.Pattern` | Parse string form |
| `from_string(s)` | `Irrep` | Construct from matched string |
| `__mul__(a, b)` | `Iterator[Irrep]` | Selection rule for tensor product |
| `clebsch_gordan(a, b, c)` | `ndarray (n, d1, d2, d3)` | CG coefficients |
| `dim` (property) | `int` | Dimension of representation |
| `iterator()` | `Iterator[Irrep]` | All irreps, trivial first |
| `continuous_generators()` | `ndarray` | Lie algebra generators |
| `discrete_generators()` | `ndarray` | Finite symmetry generators |
| `algebra()` |B `ndarray` | Structure constants |

Three built-in groups ship with the library: **`cue.SO3(l)`** (3D rotations), **`cue.O3(l, p)`** (rotations + parity), and **`cue.SU2(j)`** (spin group).

### Descriptors

Descriptors are the primary high-level interface. All come in two variants: **original** (returns `EquivariantPolynomial` with dense operands) and **`_ir_dict`** (returns `IrDictPolynomial` with operands split by irrep). Available descriptors include `fully_connected_tensor_product`, `channelwise_tensor_product`, `full_tensor_product`, `elementwise_tensor_product`, `linear`, `spherical_harmonics`, and `symmetric_contraction` (MACE-style).

Sources: [SKILL.md](library-skills/cuequivariance/SKILL.md#L7-L50), [SKILL.md](library-skills/cuequivariance/SKILL.md#L52-L115), [SKILL.md](library-skills/cuequivariance/SKILL.md#L200-L280)

##7## parabricks — Individual Tool Routing

The **parabricks** skill routes NVIDIA Parabricks `pbrun` commands, assesses GPU/runtime readiness, and provides version-aware command guidance for individual tools. It covers 26 `pbrun` sub-commands across DNA alignment, RNA-seq, variant calling, BAM QC, and GVCF workflows, each documented in a dedicated reference file under `references/`.

### Workflow and Decision Logic

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[User Request] --> B{Classify Request}
    B -->|Runtime readiness| C[runtime-environment.md]
    B -->|Tool discovery| D[tool-index.md]
    B -->|Specific command| E[references/pbrun-tool.md]
    C --> F[Run check_parabricks_runtime.py]
    D --> G[Identify correct pbrun subcommand]
    E --> H[Collect biological + filesystem context]
    G --> H
    H --> I[Generate Docker command with mounts + placeholders]
    I --> J[Validate paths, indexes, outputs]
    F --> J
```

### Runtime Readiness

The skill ships a diagnostic script `check_parabricks_runtime.py` that probes the host for GPU availability, NVIDIA driver version, CUDA compatibility, Docker access, GPU container execution, storage paths, and optional Parabricks container verification. It outputs a structured JSON report with assessments and recommendations.

### Tool Reference Architecture

Each `pbrun` tool has a dedicated reference file (e.g., `references/pbrun-fq2bam.md`) providing version-sensitive flags, I/O specifications, and command shapes. The skill's `SKILL.md` contains a 26-row routing table mapping tool name → reference file → use-when condition, ensuring agents load **only the reference for the selected tool** rather than ingesting the entire reference corpus.

Sources: [SKILL.md](library-skills/parabricks/SKILL.md#L21-L72), [SKILL.md](library-skills/parabricks/SKILL.md#L74-L162), [check_parabricks_runtime.py](library-skills/parabricks/scripts/check_parabricks_runtime.py#L1-L80)

## genomics-workflow-acceleration — Pipeline-Level GPU Wiring

The **genomics-workflow-acceleration** skill operates at a different granularity than `parabricks`: it **inspects an existing genomics workflow**, maps CPU steps to GPU equivalents, and wires **optional** GPU-accelerated steps **in place** alongside the original CPU steps — with the accelerated path **defaulting to off**.

### Supported Workflow Frameworks

| Framework | Detection Markers | Toggle Mechanism | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nextflow | `main.nf`, `nextflow.config`, `modules/`, `include {` | `params.use_parabricks` | `false` |
| Snakemake | `Snakefile`, `rules/`, `config.yaml` | `config["use_parabricks"]` | `false` |
| WDL | `*.wdl`, `workflow {`, `task`, `call` | `Boolean use_parabricks` | `false` |
| Python | `*.py`, `pyproject.toml`, CLI entrypoints | `--use-parabricks` CLI flag / `USE_PARABRICKS` env | off |

### Nine-Step Acceleration Workflow

The skill defines a rigorous nine-step process: (1) Intake and scope, (2) Runtime readiness, (3) Detect and inventory framework, (4) Map steps to Parabricks, (5) Report format, (6) Implement in place with optional accelerated steps, (7) Consolidation iteration, (8) Compare before production, (9) Optional benchmark artifacts. Each step has explicit guardrails — the skill will never delete original CPU steps, never claim bit-identical output without comparison, and always recommends a git branch before in-place edits.

### Reference Documents

Seven reference files provide domain knowledge: `parabricks-tool-map.md` (CPU → GPU mapping), `nf-core-parabricks-map.md` (Nextflow-specific module mapping), `workflow-frameworks.md` (framework detection patterns), `workflow-layout.md` (toggle naming and `ACCELERATION.md` structure), `step-consolidation.md` (merging adjacent GPU steps), `comparison-checklist.md` (toggle-off vs toggle-on validation), and `parabricks-runtime-readiness.md` (runtime assessment).

Sources: [SKILL.md](library-skills/genomics-workflow-acceleration/SKILL.md#L12-L62), [SKILL.md](library-skills/genomics-workflow-acceleration/SKILL.md#L64-L200), [parabricks-tool-map.md](library-skills/genomics-workflow-acceleration/references/parabricks-tool-map.md#L1-L49)

## Evaluation and Quality Model

Library skills use two evaluation layers. **Functional evals** (`evals.json`) verify that an agent produces correct API usage, handles edge cases, and respects guardrails. **Trigger evals** (`trigger_evals.json`) verify that the skill activates only for in-scope prompts and correctly declines out-of-scope requests.

### Functional Eval Structure

Each functional eval contains:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `id` | Unique eval identifier |
| `prompt` | The user query presented to the agent |
| `expected_output` | Natural-language description of correct behavior |
| `assertions` | List of verifiable conditions the agent's response must satisfy |
| `expected_skill` | Which skill should activate (`null` for out-of-scope) |
| `expected_script` | Diagnostic script to run (if any) |

The **assertions** are the precision mechanism — they are specific, verifiable statements about the response rather than vague quality judgments. For example, nvmolkit-usage eval `nvmolkit-usage-009` verifies that the agent recognizes tiny-batch GPU overhead, explains synchronization costs, and rewrites to batch-before-host-transfer without running a benchmark.

### Trigger Eval Example

The nvmolkit-usage trigger evals test activation boundaries:

| Prompt | Expected | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| "Port my RDKit Morgan fingerprint screen to nvMolKit" | `trigger` | Directly requests nvMolKit usage |
| "Write a pandas data cleaning script for a CSV" | `no_trigger` | No nvMolKit relevance |
| "Use RDKit for one descriptor; I have no GPU" | `no_trigger` | Single-molecule, no GPU — RDKit is correct |

Sources: [evals.json](library-skills/nvmolkit-usage/evals/evals.json#L1-L174), [trigger_evals.json](library-skills/nvmolkit-usage/evals/trigger_evals.json#L1-L31), [evals.json](library-skills/cuequivariance/evals/evals.json#L1-L58)

## Compliance and Component Registry

Library skills integrate with two downstream systems. The **component registry** (`components.d/`) maps each skill to its source repository and catalog location — for example, `components.d/nvmolkit.yml` registers the nvmolkit-usage skill under the nvMolKit component with its GitHub source and `library-skills/nvmolkit-usage` catalog path. The **compliance directory** (`compliance.d/library-skills/`) houses skill cards that document risk tiers, known risks and mitigations, output types, evaluation status, and ethical considerations in a structured format suitable for platform review and governance.

Sources: [nvmolkit.yml](components.d/nvmolkit.yml#L1-L10), [skill-card.md](compliance.d/library-skills/nvmolkit-usage/skill-card.md#L1-L72)

## Library Skills vs. Other Skill Types

Library skills occupy a distinct position in the toolkit's skill taxonomy. Understanding the boundaries prevents misrouting:

| Dimension | Library Skills | [NIM Skills](5-nim-skills) | [Open Model Skills](6-open-model-skills) |
|---|---|#---|---|
| **Target** | Python libraries, CLI tools | NIM inference endpoints | Training/fine-tuning workflows |
| **Integration point** | `import` statements, `pbrun` CLI | HTTP API calls | Training scripts, config files |
| **GPU requirement** | Varies (nvMolKit: required; cue: optional) | Required (NIM serves on GPU) | Required (training on GPU) |
| **Typical output** | Code generation + API guidance | API request construction | Training commands + configs |
| **Scope** | API-correct usage of a library | Inference on a deployed model | Full model lifecycle |
| **State** | Stateless (emits code) | Stateful (NIM deployment) | Stateful (checkpoints) |

> [!TIP]
> When a user request spans multiple skill types — for example, "use nvMolKit fingerprints as input to a MolMIM NIM" — the agent should activate the library skill for code generation and the NIM skill for inference separately, chaining outputs explicitly rather than conflating the two APIs.

Sources: [SKILL.md](library-skills/nvmolkit-usage/SKILL.md#L1-L8), [SKILL.md](library-skills/parabricks/SKILL.md#L1-L7), [SKILL.md](library-skills/genomics-workflow-acceleration/SKILL.md#L1-L10), [SKILL.md](library-skills/cuequivariance/SKILL.md#L1-L6)

## Next Steps

- To understand how library skills compare to NIM-based inference skills, see [NIM Skills](5-nim-skills).
- For the internal structure of `SKILL.md` frontmatter and2 and body, see [SKILL.md File Format](11-skill-md-file-format).
- For how evals validate skill quality, see [Evals Configuration](15-evals-configuration).
- For how skills are registered in the component registry and synced, see [Component Registry and Sync](17-component-registry-and-sync).
- For compliance and risk documentation, see [Compliance and Security Model](18-compliance-and-security-model).

# Drug Discovery Pipeline



The **Drug Discovery Pipeline** is a meta-skill that orchestrates three NVIDIA BioNeMo NIM microservices into a single computational drug discovery workflow: **GenMol** generates drug-like molecules, **DiffDock** docks them to a protein target, and **Boltz2** predicts binding affinity for the top candidates. This pipeline enables de novo hit discovery, lead optimization, and virtual screening — all composed as a sequential fan-out where each step's output feeds directly into the next.

Sources: [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/SKILL.md#L1-L221)

## Pipeline Architecture

The pipeline follows a strict three-stage fan-out topology. GenMol produces a set of SMILES strings ranked by drug-likeness (QED) or lipophilicity (LogP). Those SMILES are handed off one-by-one to DiffDock, which returns ranked docking poses with confidence scores. The top docking candidates then flow into Boltz2, which predicts structure-based pIC50 affinity and binary binding probability. The fan-out narrows at each stage: generate many molecules, dock the best subset, score only the top docking hits.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Stage1["Step 1: Molecule Generation"]
        A["SAFE Input<br/>[*{20-30}]"] --> B["GenMol NIM"]
        B --> C["SMILES + QED/LogP<br/>score"]
    end
    subgraph Stage2["Step 2: Molecular Docking"]
        C --> D["DiffDock NIM<br/>+ PDB receptor"]
        D --> E["Docked poses<br/>+ confidence"]
    end
    subgraph Stage3["Step 3: Affinity Prediction"]
        E --> F["Boltz2 NIM<br/>+ protein sequence"]
        F --> G["pIC50 + P(bind)"]
    end
    Stage1 -->|SMILES handoff| Stage2
    Stage2 -->|Top poses handoff| Stage3
```

The critical data contract between stages is the **SMILES string**: GenMol returns standard SMILES in its `molecules[].smiles` field, and those exact strings are passed as the `ligand` field (with `ligand_file_type: "txt"`) to DiffDock. Boltz2 receives the same SMILES in its `ligands[].smiles` field alongside the protein sequence.

Sources: [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/SKILL.md#L17-L26), [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/SKILL.md#L60-L93)

## Three Use Cases

| Use Case | Starting Point | GenMol Input Pattern | Pipeline Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| **De novo hit discovery** | No known scaffold | `[*{20-30}]` (masked SAFE) | Generate novel molecules from scratch, dock all candidates, score top hits |
| **Lead optimization** | Known scaffold SMILES | `safe.encode(scaffold) + ".[*{5-12}]"` | Generate analogs around the core, dock improved variants, rank by affinity |
| **Virtual screening** | Existing SMILES library | Skip GenMol; start at Step 2 | Dock the library against the target, score top docking hits with Boltz2 |

For de novo generation, GenMol requires **SAFE notation** — not raw SMILES. The `[*{min-max}]` syntax specifies a masked fragment with bounded atom counts. For scaffold-based workflows, the `safe-mol` package (`pip install safe-mol`) encodes known SMILES into SAFE notation via `safe.encode()`. Simple ring-only scaffolds may raise `SAFEFragmentationError`; fall back to the original SMILES plus a SAFE mask.

Sources: [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/SKILL.md#L28-L36), [science.md](/nim-skills/genmol-nim/references/science.md#L1-L35)

## Prerequisites and Configuration

Before executing the pipeline, confirm four parameters with the user:

1. **Target protein** — a PDB file (for DiffDock) and/or amino acid sequence (for Boltz2)
2. **Starting point** — de novo (no scaffold) or scaffold decoration (known core SMILES)
3. **Scoring metric** — `QED` (drug-likeness, 0–1) or `LogP` (lipophilicity)
4. **API mode** — hosted NVIDIA API or local Docker deployment

The pipeline requires `NGC_API_KEY` for hosted endpoints (Bearer token auth) and for local Docker registry login. When running local containers, **do not assume all three NIMs run on `localhost:8000` simultaneously**. Either run one container at a time with file-based handoffs, or start each NIM on a distinct host port and configure per-step URLs.

> [!TIP]
> When using hosted NVIDIA APIs, molecule inputs, target protein data, and your `NGC_API_KEY` are transmitted to external NVIDIA-hosted API endpoints on every call. Use local NIM containers for confidential or proprietary data.

Sources: [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/SKILL.md#L38-L53)

## Hosted vs Local Endpoints

The hosted and local endpoint paths **differ significantly** for each NIM. This is a common source of 404 errors.

| Step | NIM Skill | Hosted Endpoint | Local Endpoint |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — Generate | `genmol-nim` | `https://health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/nvidia/genmol/generate` | `http://localhost:8000/generate` |
| 2 — Dock | `diffdock-nim` | `https://health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/mit/diffdock` | `http://localhost:8000/molecular-docking/diffdock/generate` |
| 3 — Predict | `boltz2-nim` | `https://health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/mit/boltz2/predict` | `http://localhost:8000/biology/mit/boltz2/predict` |

Hosted requests require `Authorization: Bearer $NGC_API_KEY` on **every** call. Local requests use no auth header after container readiness. DiffDock's hosted path is notably different from its local path — the old `/v1/molecular-docking/diffdock/generate` hosted URL returns 404.

Sources: [api.md](/nim-skills/genmol-nim/references/api.md#L5-L8), [api.md](/nim-skills/diffdock-nim/references/api.md#L5-L10), [api.md](/nim-skills/boltz2-nim/references/api.md#L5-L8)

## Step 1: Generate Molecules with GenMol

GenMol generates drug-like molecules from SAFE notation input and returns standard SMILES with a quality score. Request more molecules than needed (e.g., 30) to compensate for post-generation filtering of invalid or duplicate structures.

```python
import requests, json, os
import safe as sf                          # pip install safe-mol
from pathlib import Path

NGC_API_KEY = os.getenv("NGC_API_KEY")
HOSTED = True

if HOSTED:
    genmol_url = "https://health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/nvidia/genmol/generate"
    headers = {"Content-Type": "application/json",
               "Authorization": f"Bearer {NGC_API_KEY}"}
else:
    genmol_url = "http://localhost:8000/generate"
    headers = {"Content-Type": "application/json"}

# De novo generation (no scaffold):
safe_input = "[*{20-30}]"

# Scaffold decoration (known core):
# scaffold_smiles = "c1ccccc1"
# safe_input = sf.encode(scaffold_smiles) + ".[*{5-10}]"

payload = {
    "smiles": safe_input,              # SAFE notation, not raw SMILES
    "num_molecules": 30,
    "scoring": "QED",                  # QED or LogP
    "unique": True,
    "temperature": "1.0",             # string, not float
    "noise": "1.0",                   # string, not float
}

r = requests.post(genmol_url, headers=headers, json=payload)
r.raise_for_status()
molecules = r.json()["molecules"]
molecules_sorted = sorted(molecules, key=lambda x: x["score"], reverse=True)
top_20 = molecules_sorted[:20]
```

### GenMol Payload Reference

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `smiles` | string | yes | SAFE notation with `[*{min-max}]` masks — **not raw SMILES** |
| `num_molecules` | integer | no | 1–1000; actual output may be fewer after filtering |
| `temperature` | **string** | no | `"0.01"`–`"10"` — **must be string, not float** |
| `noise` | **string** | no | `"0"`–`"2"` — **must be string, not float** |
| `step_size` | integer | no | 1–10; larger may reduce quality |
| `scoring` | string | no | `"QED"` (drug-likeness) or `"LogP"` (lipophilicity) |
| `unique` | boolean | no | Deduplicate output before returning |

> [!TIP]
> The `temperature` and `noise` fields in GenMol's payload must be **quoted strings** (`"1.0"`), not bare floats (`1.0`). This is an API quirk that silently fails or produces unexpected results if violated.

Sources: [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/SKILL.md#L55-L93), [api.md](/nim-skills/genmol-nim/references/api.md#L24-L49)

## Step 2: Dock Molecules with DiffDock

DiffDock performs blind molecular docking — it searches the receptor surface without requiring a user-specified binding pocket. The protein input must contain **only ATOM records** (strip HETATM, waters, and headers). Ligands from GenMol are passed as SMILES with `ligand_file_type: "txt"`.

```python
# Load protein (ATOM records only)
receptor_pdb_raw = Path("target.pdb").read_text()
receptor_pdb = "\n".join(line for line in receptor_pdb_raw.splitlines()
                          if line.startswith("ATOM"))

if HOSTED:
    diffdock_url = "https://health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/mit/diffdock"
else:
    diffdock_url = "http://localhost:8000/molecular-docking/diffdock/generate"

docking_results = []

for i, mol in enumerate(top_20):
    payload = {
        "protein": receptor_pdb,
        "ligand": mol["smiles"],
        "ligand_file_type": "txt",     # "txt" for SMILES input
        "num_poses": 5,
        "time_divisions": 20,
        "steps": 18,
        "save_trajectory": False,
    }

    r = requests.post(diffdock_url, headers=headers, json=payload)
    r.raise_for_status()
    result = r.json()

    best_conf = result["position_confidence"][0]  # rank 1 pose
    best_pose = result["ligand_positions"][0]

    docking_results.append({
        "smiles": mol["smiles"],
        "qed_score": mol["score"],
        "docking_confidence": best_conf,
        "best_pose_sdf": best_pose,
    })

# Rank by docking confidence (higher/less-negative = better)
docking_results.sort(key=lambda x: x["docking_confidence"], reverse=True)
```

### DiffDock Payload Reference

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `protein` | string | yes | PDB content — **ATOM records only** |
| `ligand` | string | yes | SMILES string or SDF/MOL2 content |
| `ligand_file_type` | string | yes | `"txt"` for SMILES, `"sdf"`, or `"mol2"` — **not `"smiles"`** |
| `num_poses` | integer | no | ≤100; number of docking poses to generate |
| `time_divisions` | integer | no | ≤20; diffusion time divisions |
| `steps` | integer | no | ≤18; diffusion steps |
| `save_trajectory` | boolean | no | Include trajectory frames in response |

### DiffDock Confidence Interpretation

DiffDock returns `position_confidence` as **negative floats**. Higher (less negative) values indicate more reliable binding pose predictions. The confidence scores are pose-ranking signals within a single response — they are **not calibrated binding free energies** and should not be reported as pIC50, Kd, or ΔG.

Sources: [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/SKILL.md#L95-L130), [api.md](/nim-skills/diffdock-nim/references/api.md#L14-L41), [science.md](/nim-skills/diffdock-nim/references/science.md#L1-L41)

## Step 3: Predict Binding Affinity with Boltz2

Boltz2 predicts biomolecular complex structures and estimates ligand binding affinity. Unlike DiffDock (which docks against an existing PDB structure), Boltz2 requires the **protein amino acid sequence** — not the PDB file. Affinity is requested by setting `predict_affinity: true` on exactly one ligand per request.

```python
if HOSTED:
    boltz_url = "https://health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/mit/boltz2/predict"
else:
    boltz_url = "http://localhost:8000/biology/mit/boltz2/predict"

target_sequence = "<YOUR_TARGET_PROTEIN_SEQUENCE>"

affinity_results = []
for d in docking_results[:5]:  # score top 5 docking hits
    payload = {
        "polymers": [
            {"id": "A", "molecule_type": "protein", "sequence": target_sequence}
        ],
        "ligands": [
            {"id": "L1", "smiles": d["smiles"], "predict_affinity": True}
        ],
        "recycling_steps": 3,
        "sampling_steps": 50,
        "diffusion_samples": 1,
        "output_format": "mmcif",
    }

    r = requests.post(boltz_url, headers=headers, json=payload)
    r.raise_for_status()
    result = r.json()

    aff = result["affinities"]["L1"]
    pic50 = aff["affinity_pic50"][0]
    prob_binding = aff["affinity_probability_binary"][0]

    affinity_results.append({
        **d,
        "pic50": pic50,
        "probability_binding": prob_binding,
    })

# Final ranking by pIC50
affinity_results.sort(key=lambda x: x["pic50"], reverse=True)
```

### Boltz2 Key Fields

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `polymers` | list | yes | Protein/DNA/RNA chains — **use `polymers`, not `sequences`** |
| `ligands` | list | no | Small molecules with `smiles` or `ccd` identifier |
| `ligands[].predict_affinity` | bool | no | Enable affinity; **max 1 ligand per request** |
| `recycling_steps` | int | no | 1–10; more = better quality, slower |
| `sampling_steps` | int | no | 10–1000; diffusion sampling steps |
| `diffusion_samples` | int | no | 1–25; number of structures to generate |

Sources: [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/SKILL.md#L132-L179), [api.md](/nim-skills/boltz2-nim/references/api.md#L14-L59)

## Interpreting Results

After all three stages complete, the pipeline produces a ranked list of drug candidates with scores from each stage. Understanding what each score means — and what it does not mean — is critical for scientific interpretation.

| Score | Source | Range | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **QED** | GenMol | 0–1 | Drug-likeness; >0.5 is considered drug-like |
| **LogP** | GenMol | ~−5 to +7 | Lipophilicity; moderate values (1–3) often preferred |
| **Docking confidence** | DiffDock | Negative floats | Higher (less negative) = more reliable pose; **not a binding free energy** |
| **pIC50** | Boltz2 | ~0–12 | Predicted −log₁₀(IC50); >6 = sub-micromolar, >8 = very potent |
| **P(bind)** | Boltz2 | 0–1 | Binary binding probability; >0.7 = likely binder |

All scores are **model estimates requiring orthogonal validation**. QED and LogP are heuristic properties, not direct activity or toxicity measurements. DiffDock confidence is a pose-ranking signal, not a calibrated affinity. Boltz2 pIC50 and P(bind) are predictions that should be confirmed with experimental assays. Generated molecules always require medicinal chemistry review, synthetic feasibility checks, and liability screening before use.

Sources: [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/SKILL.md#L183-L190), [science.md](/nim-skills/genmol-nim/references/science.md#L14-L22), [science.md](/nim-skills/boltz2-nim/references/science.md#L17-L23)

## Pipeline Gotchas and Critical Type Requirements

The pipeline has several non-obvious API contract requirements that are validated in the evaluation suite. Violating any of these produces silent failures or 422 errors.

| Gotcha | Stage | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| SAFE notation required | GenMol | The `smiles` field accepts SAFE notation, not raw SMILES. De novo uses `[*{20-30}]`; scaffolds must be encoded with `safe-mol` |
| String-typed numerics | GenMol | `temperature` and `noise` must be strings (`"1.0"`), not floats (`1.0`) |
| `ligand_file_type: "txt"` | DiffDock | SMILES input uses `"txt"`, not `"smiles"` or `"sdf"` |
| ATOM records only | DiffDock | Strip HETATM, waters, and headers from PDB before sending |
| `polymers` not `sequences` | Boltz2 | The protein input field is `polymers`; using `sequences` fails with 422 |
| `predict_affinity: true` | Boltz2 | Must be explicitly set on the ligand; max one affinity ligand per request |
| Protein sequence not PDB | Boltz2 | Boltz2 needs the amino acid sequence, not the PDB file content |
| Hosted ≠ local paths | DiffDock | Hosted: `/v1/biology/mit/diffdock`; local: `/molecular-docking/diffdock/generate` |
| Bearer auth on all hosted | All | Every hosted request needs `Authorization: Bearer $NGC_API_KEY` |

Sources: [evals.json](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/evals/evals.json#L1-L167)

## Local Docker Deployment

When running the pipeline locally, each NIM runs in its own Docker container with specific GPU, memory, and cache requirements. The containers are started independently, and the pipeline coordinates calls between them.

| NIM | Image | Min GPU VRAM | `--shm-size` | Cache Size |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GenMol | `nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/genmol:1.0.1` | 16 GB | 2G | ~20 GB |
| DiffDock | `nvcr.io/nim/mit/diffdock:2.2.0` | 24 GB | 2G | ~40 GB |
| Boltz2 | `nvcr.io/nim/mit/boltz2:1.6.0` | 16 GB | 16G | ~30 GB |

All containers require `--runtime=nvidia`, `--ulimit memlock=-1`, `--ulimit stack=67108664`, and the `NGC_API_KEY` environment variable for first-run model downloads. Wait for readiness on `http://localhost:<port>/v1/health/ready` before sending inference requests. Local inference requests use **no auth header** after readiness.

For detailed Docker startup commands, refer to the individual NIM skill references: [GenMol api.md](/nim-skills/genmol-nim/references/api.md#L131-L159), [DiffDock api.md](/nim-skills/diffdock-nim/references/api.md#L97-L126), [Boltz2 api.md](/nim-skills/boltz2-nim/references/api.md#L8-L12).

Sources: [api.md](/nim-skills/genmol-nim/references/api.md#L163-L190), [api.md](/nim-skills/diffdock-nim/references/api.md#L140-L156)

## Evaluation and Quality Assurance

The drug-discovery-pipeline meta-skill includes a comprehensive evaluation suite that validates correct pipeline composition, API contract adherence, and data handoff integrity. The eval configuration uses the `aces_default` grading mode with `NGC_API_KEY` as the required runtime environment variable.

| Eval ID | Scenario | Key Assertions |
|---|---|---|
| `eval-1-de-novo-hit-discovery` | Full hosted pipeline with EGFR receptor | SAFE notation, string temperature/noise, `ligand_file_type: "txt"`, ATOM-only protein, `polymers` field, SMILES handoff |
| `eval-2-lead-optimization-scaffold` (deferred) | Scaffold decoration for CDK2 | SAFE encoding of known SMILES, correct hosted URLs, ATOM filtering, `predict_affinity` flag, pIC50 extraction |
| `eval-3-docking-affinity-scoring` (deferred) | Docking + affinity only (no GenMol) | Negative confidence interpretation, `ligand_file_type: "txt"`, correct local endpoint, `polymers` field, `affinity_probability_binary` extraction, Bearer auth |
| `eval-4-full-hosted-pipeline` (deferred) | Complete Python script for all three stages | Exact hosted URLs for all three NIMs, Bearer auth on every request, string-typed GenMol params, top-hits selection with `polymers` field |

Sources: [evals.json](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/evals/evals.json#L1-L167), [config.yml](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/evals/config.yml#L1-L10)

For API-specific payload details, Docker flags, and scientific limitations beyond what the pipeline documents, consult the individual skill references.

| Step | Skill Name | Location | Key Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `genmol-nim` | `nim-skills/genmol-nim/` | [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/genmol-nim/SKILL.md#L1-L127) |
| 2 | `diffdock-nim` | `nim-skills/diffdock-nim/` | [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/diffdock-nim/SKILL.md#L1-L119) |
| 3 | `boltz2-nim` | `nim-skills/boltz2-nim/` | [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/boltz2-nim/SKILL.md#L1-L147) |

Sources: [SKILL.md](/nim-skills/meta-skills/drug-discovery-pipeline/SKILL.md#L192-L198), [README.md](/nim-skills/meta-skills/README.md#L1-L15)

- Learn about the evaluation framework: [Skill Lift Evaluation](14-skill-lift-evaluation)

# Protein Binder Design Workflow



The **Generative Protein Binder Design** workflow provides two independent, composable skill routes for *de novo* protein binder design — each resolving a target structure and hotspots, generating candidate binders, independently co-folding the binder–target complex with a structure predictor, and ranking by interface confidence metrics. The two routes differ in their **generation paradigm**: one uses NVIDIA's Proteina-Complexa for reward-guided co-design of sequence+structure together; the other composes BioNeMo NIMs (RFdiffusion → ProteinMPNN → Boltz2/OpenFold3) in the classic diffusion + inverse-folding pipeline. Both converge on the same validation philosophy: an **independent** structure predictor grades what the generator produced, preventing self-evaluation bias.

Sources: [README.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/README.md#L1-L16), [workflow-rules.mdc](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/workflow-rules.mdc#L1-L36)

## Route Selection

The workflow exposes two skills, selected by the user's preferred generation approach and available backend:

| Dimension | `complexa-binder-design` | `protein-binder-design` |
|---|---|---|
| **Generator** | Proteina-Complexa (reward-guided co-design of sequence+structure) | RFdiffusion backbones → ProteinMPNN sequences |
| **Selection** | Internal AF2-reward gate + test-time search (best-of-n / beam / FK / MCTS) | Filter by co-fold interface metrics |
| **Independent validation** | Boltz2 (default) or OpenFold3 co-fold | Boltz2 / OpenFold3 co-fold |
| **Ranking metrics** | interface confidence, pLDDT, ipSAE, apo/holo stability, hotspot contact | ipTM / ipSAE / pLDDT / apo↔holo RMSD |
| **Backend** | Proteina-Complexa (local) + Boltz2 NIM | BioNeMo NIMs (RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN, Boltz2/OpenFold3) |
| **Prefer when** | User asks for Proteina-Complexa / reward-guided search | User wants the RFdiffusion + ProteinMPNN NIM pipeline |

Pick based on the generator the user wants (Proteina-Complexa vs RFdiffusion/ProteinMPNN) or which backend is available. Both resolve target + hotspots first, generate binders, co-fold the complex with an independent predictor, and rank by interface metrics.

Sources: [route-selection.mdc](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/references/route-selection.mdc#L1-L26)

## Architecture Overview

The following diagram illustrates how both routes share a common four-stage skeleton — target resolution, generation, independent validation, and report — while differing in their generation and selection internals:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Common["Shared Skeleton"]
        T["Stage 1: Resolve Target + Hotspots"] --> G["Stage 2: Generate Binders"]
        G --> V["Stage 3: Independent Validation (Co-fold + Gate)"]
        V --> R["Stage 4: Filter + Rank + Report"]
    end

    subgraph RouteA["complexa-binder-design"]
        direction TB
        CX["Proteina-Complexa CLI<br/>co-design seq+structure"]
        AF2["AF2-reward gate<br/>(best-of-n / beam / MCTS)"]
        CX --> AF2
    end

    subgraph RouteB["protein-binder-design"]
        direction TB
        RFD["RFdiffusion NIM<br/>backbone PDBs"]
        PMPNN["ProteinMPNN NIM<br/>k sequences per backbone"]
        RFD --> PMPNN
    end

    subgraph Validate["Independent Validation"]
        direction TB
        B2["Boltz2 NIM<br/>holo + apo refold"]
        OF3["OpenFold3 NIM<br/>(optional)"]
    end

    G -.->|"Route A"| CX
    G -.->|"Route B"| RFD
    AF2 --> V
    PMPNN --> V
    V --> B2
    V --> OF3
```

> [!TIP]
> Both routes validate with a **different model family** than the generator — Complexa's AF2 reward is not the final judge (Boltz2/OpenFold3 is), and RFdiffusion/ProteinMPNN outputs are independently co-folded. This "generator ≠ validator" principle is the core quality guarantee.

Sources: [workflow-rules.mdc](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/workflow-rules.mdc#L1-L36), [protein-binder-design SKILL.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/SKILL.md#L1-L117), [complexa-binder-design SKILL.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/complexa-binder-design/SKILL.md#L1-L200)

---

## Route A: protein-binder-design (RFdiffusion + ProteinMPNN + Boltz2/OpenFold3)

This skill composes atomic BioNeMo NIMs into a sequential pipeline: diffuse binder backbones, design sequences onto those backbones, co-fold each binder with the target, and rank by interface quality. The skill owns orchestration, handoff contracts, filtering, validation, and the run manifest — it does **not** duplicate per-NIM API details, deferring those to each atomic skill's own `SKILL.md`.

### Composed NIM Skills

| Step | Skill | Owns |
|---|---|---|
| Backbones | `rfdiffusion-nim` | binder backbone PDBs (contigs + hotspots) |
| Sequences | `proteinmpnn-nim` | sequences for each backbone |
| Co-fold / score | `boltz2-nim` or `openfold3-nim` | binder–target complex + confidence / ipTM |
| MSA (optional) | `msa-search-nim` | target A3M for higher-quality folding |

The atomic NIM skills are **recommended companions** but not strictly required — `references/pipeline.md` carries the concrete request shape for every NIM call, so an agent with NIM access can follow this skill standalone.

### Pipeline Stages

**Stage 1 — Target prep:** Obtain the target PDB and epitope; map epitope/hotspot author residue numbers to RFdiffusion `hotspot_res` strings; optionally build a target MSA with `msa-search-nim`. A human-in-the-loop gate confirms target chain, epitope/hotspot set, binder length range, and hosted-vs-local before proceeding.

**Stage 2 — Backbones (RFdiffusion):** Generate N binder backbone PDBs using the target `input_pdb`, a contig combining the target segment and a generated binder segment (e.g. `"E1-200/0 60-90"`), and `hotspot_res` strings like `["E453", "E455", "E486"]`:

```python
payload = {
    "input_pdb": target_pdb,
    "contigs": "E1-200/0 60-90",
    "hotspot_res": ["E453", "E455", "E456", "E486", "E489", "E493", "E501"],
    "diffusion_steps": 50,
}
```

**Stage 3 — Sequences (ProteinMPNN):** For each backbone, design k sequences redesigning the **binder chain only** (`input_pdb_chains=[binder_chain]`) so the target chain stays fixed. **Drop the native/WT row** from `mfasta` and pair scores only with designed rows:

```python
payload = {
    "input_pdb": backbone_pdb,
    "input_pdb_chains": [binder_chain],
    "num_seq_per_target": 8,
    "sampling_temp": [0.1, 0.2],
    "use_soluble_model": True,
}
```

**Stage 4 — Co-fold + score (Boltz2 / OpenFold3):** Co-fold each designed binder with the target as a 2-chain complex. OpenFold3 returns explicit `iptm_score`; Boltz2 returns `confidence_scores` as the fallback complex-confidence signal.

**Stage 5 — Self-consistency RMSD:** Compare the RFdiffusion backbone to the predicted binder chain from the co-folded complex using Kabsch CA-RMSD (`scripts/metrics.py`). Low RMSD indicates the sequence is predicted to fold back into the designed backbone.

**Stage 6 — Filter + rank + report:** Apply thresholds, rank survivors, write manifest + CSV.

### Handoff Contracts

The glue between NIM steps is the most fragile part of the pipeline. Key contracts:

- **RFdiffusion `output_pdb` → ProteinMPNN `input_pdb`** (inline PDB text).
- **ProteinMPNN `mfasta` → Boltz2 binder polymer `sequence`** (exclude the native/WT row; pair scores only with designed rows).
- **Epitope author residue numbers → 1-based sequence indices:** remap with `scripts/pdb_utils.py:remap_to_seq_index`. RFdiffusion `hotspot_res` uses chain+author strings like `"A50"`; Boltz2 pocket/contacts use 1-based indices.
- **Boltz2 complex `.cif` → binder chain → self-consistency RMSD** vs the backbone.

### Default Filters

| Metric | Threshold | Source |
|---|---|---|
| ipTM | ≥ 0.8 | OpenFold3 `iptm_score` / Boltz2 `confidence_scores` |
| Binder pLDDT | ≥ 80 | OpenFold3 / Boltz2 |
| Self-consistency RMSD | ≤ 2.0 Å | `scripts/metrics.py` (Kabsch CA-RMSD) |

Override per campaign and record overrides in the manifest `filters` field.

### Validation Methodology

Always run controls and report a **success rate**, not just top scores. **Negative controls** use composition-preserving scrambled sequences (`scripts/controls.py`); **positive controls** re-score published binders through the identical pipeline. Benchmark targets live in `assets/targets.json` (`scripts/registry.py`). The success rate (fraction of designs passing the filter) is the primary metric for comparing pipeline configurations — absolute scores are not comparable across pipelines.

### Run Manifest

Every campaign writes `manifest.json` + `candidates.csv` under a run directory via `scripts/manifest.py`. The manifest records lineage, params, scores, artifacts, filter status, and controls — enabling ranking, resumability, validation, and the final report:

```text
runs/<campaign>_<date>/
├── manifest.json          # campaign state
├── candidates.csv         # flat table, regenerated from the manifest
├── backbones/             # RFdiffusion output PDBs
├── sequences/             # ProteinMPNN mfasta files
└── complexes/             # Boltz2/OpenFold3 co-folded .cif files
```

The manifest is resumable — an interrupted campaign reloads it and skips candidates that already have the needed scores/artifacts.

Sources: [protein-binder-design SKILL.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/SKILL.md#L1-L117), [pipeline.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/references/pipeline.md#L1-L152), [manifest.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/references/manifest.md#L1-L72), [validation.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/references/validation.md#L1-L70), [manifest.py](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/scripts/manifest.py#L1-L180), [metrics.py](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/scripts/metrics.py#L1-L40), [pdb_utils.py](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/scripts/pdb_utils.py#L1-L92), [controls.py](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/scripts/controls.py#L1-L27)

---

## Route B: complexa-binder-design (Proteina-Complexa + Boltz2/OpenFold3)

This skill uses NVIDIA's **Proteina-Complexa** — an open model that **co-designs binder sequence + full-atom structure together** (no inverse-folding step) with reward-guided test-time search. Validation uses a **different** model family (Boltz2 / OpenFold3), so the headline confidence is an independent check, not the generator grading its own homework.

### Upstream Model (User-Provided)

- **Code:** [github.com/NVIDIA-Digital-Bio/Proteina-Complexa](https://github.com/NVIDIA-Digital-Bio/Proteina-Complexa) (the `complexa` CLI)
- **Weights (NGC):** `nvidia/clara/proteina_complexa`
- **Paper:** Didi et al., *Scaling Atomistic Protein Binder Design…*, ICLR 2026
- **First-time setup:** `references/setup.md` — full standalone install with **no NIM** required for generation

### Pipeline Stages

**Stage 1 — Resolve target + hotspots (no GPU):** The user provides a target as a name, sequence, and/or structure file. The skill resolves exactly **one** design-ready structure in priority order: (1) experimental PDB (RCSB), (2) AFDB model (UniProt), (3) user-provided file, (4) fold de novo. Hotspots resolve in evidence order:

1. **PDB co-complex interface** (gold standard) — interface residues from a structure where the target contacts a protein partner
2. **UniProt functional residues** — `Mutagenesis` + accessible `Active/Binding/Site`, filtered to the extracellular/accessible range
3. **Literature (Paperclip)** — full-text mining when 1–2 are empty
4. **Unconditioned** (`[]`) only as a documented last resort

Deterministic enforcement then applies: **structure alignment** (drop residues absent from the coordinate file, read back real 3-letter identity), **epitope sanity** (drop outliers > 30 Å from cluster centroid, cap at 15 residues), and **size budget ≤ 500 residues** (Complexa builds an O(n²) pair-feature map over the whole complex). **Preflight** (`scripts/preflight_design.py`) reports the conditioned length, re-aligned hotspots, compactness, budget, and a READY / NEEDS-ATTENTION verdict — review before spending GPU.

**Stage 2 — Generate (Proteina-Complexa CLI):** Register the target, then use `complexa generate` (NOT the full `complexa design`) with reward-guided `best-of-n`:

```bash
python scripts/complexa_design.py run --task-name <name> --run-name <run> \
    --algorithm best-of-n --num-samples <N> --seed 0 --out <run-dir>
```

Search algorithms: `best-of-n` (default) · `beam-search` · `fk-steering` · `mcts`. The AF2 reward (configured via `setup_af2_params.sh` + `AF2_DIR`) AF2-selects the best candidates **during generation** and writes co-designed sequence + structure PDBs to `inference/`. **Use the sequence directly — do not MPNN-redesign it.**

> [!TIP]
> **Do NOT run the full `complexa design`** for this workflow. Its `evaluate` stage re-folds every design with AF2/RF3/ESMFold (redundant — best-of-n already AF2-selected during search) and its `analyze` stage needs `foldseek`/`sc` (usually not installed). The lean `generate` → independent Boltz2 validation is the intended path. No AF2 params? Use `--af2-bypass` and let the Boltz2 gate select.

**Stage 3 — Validate (independent refold + gate):** Per binder, run **two** predictions with one refolder (Boltz2 default): **holo** (binder + target; target MSA, binder single-sequence, `write_full_pae`) and **apo** (binder alone). `scripts/boltz2_refold.py` makes holo calls (retry/backoff for rate limits), then chains `scripts/validate_binders.py` for apo + metrics + gate + rank.

**Stage 4 — Gate + rank + report:** Apply the strict gate, rank survivors, write `ranked_binders.json`/`.csv`, and produce the report.

### Validation Gates (complexa route)

Every gate must hold for a design to pass:

| Metric | Gate | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| ipTM | ≥ 0.65 | predicted interface quality |
| Complex pLDDT | ≥ 0.70 | overall complex fold confidence |
| Binder pLDDT (holo) | ≥ 0.70 | binder fold confidence in complex |
| Apo binder pLDDT | ≥ 0.70 | binder fold confidence alone |
| ipSAE (min) | ≥ 0.45 | min interface-pSAE over binder↔target |
| Apo↔holo binder RMSD | ≤ 2.5 Å | pre-organization / rigidity signal |
| Hotspot contact | ≥ 20% | fraction of conditioned hotspots contacted (CB–CB < 13 Å) |

**Per-chain conditioning:** binder = single-sequence, no MSA, no template (de novo); target = MSA (via `msa-search-nim` or `scripts/fetch_target_msa_colabfold.py`), optional structural template (via `scripts/pdb_to_boltz_template_cif.py`). Validation is **always unconditioned** — the holo refold receives only sequences, never the hotspot list; hotspot contact is then an independent geometric test.

### Bounded-Budget Loop

The deliverable is **top-N binders ranked by interface confidence** (default 10). Run **at most 2 generation rounds**, then deliver the top-N by score even if fewer than N clear the strict gate — keep each design's `pass`/`failure_reason` flag. **Do not** keep generating just to chase N strict passes. Stop on: N-passed / 2 rounds / budget exhausted / ≥3 consecutive zero-passer rounds. A persistent 0% pass rate is a scientific signal (bad hotspots/length/algorithm) — surface it and propose changes.

### Output Layout

```text
outputs/<target>_<run_id>/
├── target.pdb / target.cif
├── hotspots.json
├── design/                     # Complexa complex PDBs + run config
├── sequences/                  # binder sequences extracted from complexes
├── validation/holo/ , validation/apo/
├── ranked_binders.json / .csv  # every design (pass+fail), all metrics
├── REPORT_<target>_<run_id>.md
└── manifest.json
```

Sources: [complexa-binder-design SKILL.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/complexa-binder-design/SKILL.md#L1-L200), [complexa pipeline.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/complexa-binder-design/references/pipeline.md#L1-L124), [complexa validation.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/complexa-binder-design/references/validation.md#L1-L81), [pipeline.py](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/complexa-binder-design/scripts/pipeline.py#L1-L200)

---

## NIM Configuration (Hosted vs Local)

Each NIM in the pipeline is reached over HTTP. Choose **hosted** or **local** once and reuse for every call:

| NIM | Hosted Endpoint | Local Port | Idle GPU | Docker Image |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RFdiffusion | `health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/ipd/rfdiffusion/generate` | 8081 | ~24 GB | `nvcr.io/nim/ipd/rfdiffusion:latest` |
| ProteinMPNN | `health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/ipd/proteinmpnn/predict` | 8082 | ~1.5 GB | `nvcr.io/nim/ipd/proteinmpnn:latest` |
| Boltz2 | `health.api.nvidia.com/v1/biology/mit/boltz2/predict` | 8083 | ~8 GB | `nvcr.io/nim/mit/boltz2:latest` |

**Hosted:** set `NVIDIA_API_KEY` (sent as `Authorization: Bearer`). Read keys from the environment — never hardcode them.

**Local:** point each NIM at its local URL (e.g. `http://localhost:8000/...`); no auth header needed. All three NIMs co-fit on one ≥48 GB GPU (~33 GB idle together). Launch each with a persistent cache volume (`/opt/nim/.cache`) so weights download once. Some NIMs (e.g. Boltz2) need `NIM_MODEL_PROFILE` pinned on GPUs with no bundled profile; others (RFdiffusion/ProteinMPNN) auto-select by compute capability.

Sources: [local-nim-setup.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/references/local-nim-setup.md#L1-L81), [rfdiffusion-nim SKILL.md](/nim-skills/rfdiffusion-nim/SKILL.md#L1-L164), [proteinmpnn-nim SKILL.md](/nim-skills/proteinmpnn-nim/SKILL.md#L1-L115), [boltz2-nim SKILL.md](/nim-skills/boltz2-nim/SKILL.md#L1-L147)

---

## Cost Funnel and Human-in-the-Loop

Co-folding is the expensive stage in both routes. Key cost discipline patterns:

- **protein-binder-design:** Co-fold a **capped shortlist** first (e.g. best ProteinMPNN NLL per backbone), review, then expand. Reserve high `recycling_steps`/`diffusion_samples` for final survivors.
- **complexa-binder-design:** Validate only ~**2× the requested N** top candidates by generation/AF2 reward — validating the entire pool wastes GPU/time and trips hosted rate limits.
- **Human-in-the-loop:** Confirm target, epitope/hotspots, binder length range, and hosted-vs-local **before** generating backbones. State the deployment mode once and reuse across all NIM calls.

Sources: [pipeline.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/references/pipeline.md#L93-L110), [complexa SKILL.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/complexa-binder-design/SKILL.md#L89-L105)

---

|---|---|

| `scripts/metrics.py` | Kabsch CA-RMSD for self-consistency |
| `scripts/controls.py` | Composition-preserving scrambled negative controls |

| Script | Purpose |
|---|---|

| `scripts/preflight_design.py` | No-GPU target/hotspot/size planner with READY verdict |
| `scripts/hotspot_strategy.py` | Evidence-based hotspot resolution |
| `scripts/pdb_interface.py` | PDB co-complex interface residue extraction |
| `scripts/complexa_design.py` | Thin `complexa generate` driver + output extraction |
| `scripts/boltz2_refold.py` | Holo Boltz2 refolds (retry/backoff + throttle) → chains validator |
| `scripts/validate_binders.py` | Apo + ipSAE + apo↔holo RMSD + hotspot contact + gating + ranking |
| `scripts/setup_af2_params.sh` | Download AF2-Multimer params (public, no auth) |
| `scripts/check_setup.sh` | One-shot environment readiness checklist |

Sources: [protein-binder-design SKILL.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/SKILL.md#L105-L117), [complexa-binder-design SKILL.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/complexa-binder-design/SKILL.md#L151-L198)

---

## Responsible Use

De novo binder design is dual-use. Both skills decline requests aimed at enhancing pathogen fitness, toxin potency, or bioweapon function; designs are kept to legitimate research and therapeutic intent.

Sources: [protein-binder-design SKILL.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/protein-binder-design/SKILL.md#L99-L102), [complexa-binder-design SKILL.md](/workflows/generative-protein-binder-design/complexa-binder-design/SKILL.md#L195-L198)
